title: Lafayette Square Gassing - Violence for Photo Op
description_short: Lafayette Square Gassing - Violence for Photo Op
description_medium: On June 1, 2020, federal officers used chemical irritants and other force to clear Lafayette Square protesters before Donald Trump walked to St. John’s Church and posed with a Bible. A later Park Police review said the plan was to install fencing; it did not establish a photo-op motive or the full chain of command.
description_long: On June 1, 2020, Donald Trump ordered federal law enforcement to use tear gas, rubber bullets, and violent force to clear peaceful protesters from Lafayette Square so he could walk to St. John's Church for a photo opportunity holding a Bible. The attack on peaceful demonstrators protesting police brutality occurred just before the city's 7 PM curfew, giving protesters no time to disperse voluntarily. Mounted police, U.S. Park Police, and federal agents in riot gear charged into the crowd of peaceful protesters, clergy, and journalists, using chemical irritants and physical force to create a path for Trump's publicity stunt. The violent clearing allowed Trump to walk from the White House to the historic church, where he awkwardly held up a Bible for photographers while making no statement about racial justice, police brutality, or the protesters' concerns. The imagery was deeply disturbing: an American president using violence against peaceful citizens exercising their First Amendment rights to create a campaign photo. Episcopal Bishop Mariann Budde, whose diocese includes St. John's Church, condemned Trump's visit, saying she was 'outraged' that he would use the church as a prop after ordering attacks on peaceful protesters. The Lafayette Square gassing became a defining image of Trump's presidency - his willingness to use state violence against American citizens for personal political theater. International observers compared the scene to tactics used by authoritarian regimes against their own people, marking a new low in presidential abuse of power.

title: SAVE Program Weaponized to Flag 67 Million Voter Registrations as Suspect
description_short: SAVE Program Weaponized to Flag 67 Million Voter Registrations as Suspect
description_medium: AP reported that at least 25 states used the expanded federal SAVE system to compare voter rolls with citizenship records, scanning 67 million registrations. A federal judge blocked the use, citing privacy risks and the possibility that eligible voters could be wrongly removed. AP also described Anthony Nel, a U.S. citizen whose Texas registration was temporarily canceled after the system flagged him.
description_long: By May 2026, the Trump administration had run at least 67 million voter registrations — primarily from Republican-controlled states that agreed to share data — through a dramatically expanded version of the DHS Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (SAVE) program. Originally designed to verify immigration status for benefits programs, SAVE was overhauled in spring 2025 to enable bulk scanning of state voter rolls against federal citizenship databases. The expanded system flagged tens of thousands of registrations as potential noncitizens or deceased persons, with some states then suspending those voters' eligibility with as little as 30 days to respond. The nonpartisan Institute for Responsive Government noted that historically 16% of SAVE searches required manual verification, meaning hundreds of thousands of legitimate citizens could face erroneous flags. A federal judge blocked the modified SAVE tool in June 2026. Maine Secretary of State Shenna Bellows said DHS told her it planned to retain all uploaded state voter data for 10 years for audit purposes, raising concerns about a de facto federal voter database built through the backdoor.

title: FEC operates without a quorum for nearly 80% of Trump's second term
description_short: FEC operates without a quorum for nearly 80% of Trump's second term
description_medium: Trump sent longtime Democratic FEC commissioner Ellen Weintraub a January 31, 2025 letter purporting to remove her; Weintraub disputed the legality of the action. After additional commissioner departures, the FEC fell below its four-member voting threshold on May 1, 2025. NOTUS reported in March 2026 that the agency had 195 pending enforcement matters and later calculated that it had lacked a quorum for nearly 80% of Trump's second term. The prolonged lack of quorum prevented substantive enforcement votes.
description_long: President Donald Trump sent Federal Election Commission Commissioner Ellen Weintraub a letter on Jan. 31, 2025, purporting to remove her. Weintraub disputed the move’s legality. After additional commissioner departures, the six-member FEC fell below the four members required for a quorum on May 1. Without a quorum, the commission could not take substantive enforcement votes, leaving complaints and investigations pending while it lacked enough members to act. NOTUS reported in March 2026 that 195 enforcement matters were pending and later calculated that the FEC had lacked a quorum for nearly 80% of Trump’s second term. Those figures show the size of the backlog and the duration of the agency’s limited voting capacity; they do not establish that the backlog resulted entirely from Weintraub’s removal or that every pending matter concerned the president. The FEC announced Commissioner Allen Dickerson’s departure on April 30, just before the commission fell below its voting threshold. The episode combined a disputed removal with later vacancies that left the campaign-finance regulator unable to make certain enforcement decisions.

title: Operation Epic Fury: Trump's Iran War Begins Without Congressional Authorization, Ends in Chaos
description_short: Operation Epic Fury: Trump's Iran War Begins Without Congressional Authorization, Ends in Chaos
description_medium: U.S. and Israeli forces began Operation Epic Fury with strikes on Iran on Feb. 28, 2026. The linked Senate resolution states that Congress had not declared war or specifically authorized force and challenges the administration’s authority. The supplied source supports the launch and authorization dispute, but not the campaign’s later duration, casualties or outcomes.
description_long: On February 28, 2026, U.S. and Israeli forces launched coordinated strikes on Iran — Operation Epic Fury — without a congressional declaration of war or AUMF, with Trump claiming the goal was to eliminate imminent threats from the Iranian regime. The 39-day bombing campaign killed Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei and dozens of Iranian military leaders but failed to achieve regime change, force denuclearization, or stop Iran's missile program. After an initial ceasefire collapsed, Trump signed a Memorandum of Understanding with Iran on June 18, 2026, at Versailles — widely condemned as appeasement — pledging billions in sanctions relief and reconstruction assistance in exchange for Iran reopening the Strait of Hormuz. When Iran resumed attacks on merchant shipping in July 2026, Trump declared the deal over and authorized new strikes, plunging the region back into conflict. The Strait of Hormuz remained partially closed — a chokepoint for 20% of the world's oil and gas — while 60% of Americans told Quinnipiac pollsters the Iran war was not worth it. Council on Foreign Relations analysts concluded Trump had launched a war of choice with no exit strategy, no congressional authorization, and no viable military path to his stated objectives.

title: Medicaid Cuts Target Disabled Americans: $900B Slashed, States Begin Re-Institutionalizing
description_short: Medicaid Cuts Target Disabled Americans: $900B Slashed, States Begin Re-Institutionalizing
description_medium: The reconciliation law signed July 4, 2025, is projected to reduce federal Medicaid spending by about $911 billion over a decade, according to the cited KFF analysis. That estimate describes federal spending, not service losses for particular people. The linked analysis does not establish the entry’s claims about home-care cuts, reinstitutionalization or later Justice Department policy.
description_long: The One Big Beautiful Bill Act signed July 4, 2025 cut a projected $900 billion-plus from Medicaid over a decade, and the June 2026 DOJ Olmstead opinion signaled the end of federal enforcement of community integration for people with disabilities. Iowa and other states began quietly reducing home health aide coverage and in-home support services that allow disabled people to avoid institutionalization. The Trump administration moved oversight of special education from the Department of Education to the Department of Health and Human Services under RFK Jr., whose public statements dismissing the severity of conditions like autism drew sharp rebukes from disability advocates. New Medicaid work requirements taking effect January 1, 2027 are expected to strip coverage from people with disabilities who cannot navigate complex exemption bureaucracies. Sen. Tammy Duckworth called the combination of cuts and DOJ opinion an attack on one of the most basic civil rights of Americans with disabilities.
organization_tags: Department of Health and Human Services
